prompt.context: Marie's Café is a small local coffee shop that serves coffee and latte. Marie's has been around for decades and is known for its high quality drinks and cozy atmosphere. The café has seen declining profits over the last few quarters, and the owner has hired you to increase its profits. There are two other coffee shops in the nearby area that sell coffees and pastries. Café currently serves two items (coffee and latte) in three different sizes. Each customer only purchases one drink per visit.
prompt.question: How would you increase profits at Marie's Café?

clarifying_info.q: What sizes does the café offer?
clarifying_info.a: Three sizes: 8 oz, 12 oz, and 16 oz for both coffee and latte.

clarifying_info.q: What are the prices of each product?
clarifying_info.a: Coffee 8oz $1.00, Coffee 12oz $1.50, Coffee 16oz $2.00; Latte 8oz $3.00, Latte 12oz $4.00, Latte 16oz $5.00.

clarifying_info.q: What are the costs to produce each drink?
clarifying_info.a: Cup costs: 8oz $0.30, 12oz $0.40, 16oz $0.50. Ingredient costs: 4oz coffee $0.10, 4oz latte $0.50 (incremental per size).

clarifying_info.q: What are the café's operating hours?
clarifying_info.a: 7AM to 10PM, Monday through Friday. Closed on weekends.

clarifying_info.q: How many baristas are on staff?
clarifying_info.a: Two baristas are working at any given time, each paid $15/hour.

clarifying_info.q: How long does it take to serve a customer?
clarifying_info.a: On average 2 minutes per order. Coffee is served quickly; lattes take significantly longer.

exhibits.title: Product Prices and Customer Mix
exhibits.shows: A table listing each product (Coffee 8oz, 12oz, 16oz and Latte 8oz, 12oz, 16oz) with its price and the percentage of customers who purchase that product.

exhibits.title: Product Costs
exhibits.shows: A table listing cup costs by size and ingredient costs per 4oz serving for coffee and latte.

exhibits.title: Average Customer Demand by Hour
exhibits.shows: A table listing average demand (number of customers) per hour across five time blocks throughout the day.

framework: Revenue drivers: product mix (coffee vs latte, size), pricing, volume of customers served
Cost drivers: variable costs (ingredients, cups) per product, labor costs (baristas)
Capacity constraints: barista throughput (2 min/order, max 30 orders/barista/hour), hours of operation
Competitive context: two nearby competitors selling coffee and pastries — product gap opportunity
Growth levers: optimize product mix toward higher-margin items, adjust staffing to demand, add new products/services

questions.prompt: How much profit does Marie's Café currently make per customer?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate cost per product (cup cost + ingredient cost), then profit per product, then weight by purchase percentage to get average profit per customer. Strong candidates note that larger sizes have higher margins and suggest strategies to shift the mix toward larger sizes (upsell, eliminate 8oz, introduce 20oz).

math.setup: Cost per product = cup cost + ingredient cost. Ingredient cost scales with size: 8oz uses 2×4oz = $0.20 coffee/$1.00 latte; 12oz uses 3×4oz = $0.30 coffee/$1.50 latte; 16oz uses 4×4oz = $0.40 coffee/$2.00 latte. Total cost = cup cost + ingredient cost. Profit = Price - Cost. Weighted average profit = sum of (profit × % customers).

questions.prompt: What is the average profit that Marie's Café earns per day (with current 2-barista staffing)?
questions.guidance: Candidate must identify the capacity constraint: 2 baristas × 30 orders/hour (60 seconds/min × 1 order/2 min) = 60 customers/hour max. Customers leave if not served quickly, so demand above 60 is lost. For each time block, actual served = min(demand, 60). Revenue per hour = served × $1.50 profit. Labor cost = 2 baristas × $15/hour. Net profit per block = (served × $1.50) - (2 × $15 × hours). Candidate should flag the 7PM-10PM block is unprofitable.

math.setup: Capacity = 2 baristas × 30 orders/hour = 60 customers/hour. Each time block is 3 hours. Net profit per block = (min(demand,60) × $1.50 - 2 × $15) × 3 hours.
steps: 7AM-10AM (3hrs): served=60, revenue=60×$1.50=$90/hr, labor=2×$15=$30/hr, net/hr=$60, block profit=$60×3=$180
10AM-1PM (3hrs): served=60, revenue=$90/hr, labor=$30/hr, net/hr=$60, block profit=$180
1PM-4PM (3hrs): served=60, revenue=$90/hr, labor=$30/hr, net/hr=$60, block profit=$180
4PM-7PM (3hrs): served=40, revenue=40×$1.50=$60/hr, labor=$30/hr, net/hr=$30, block profit=$30×3=$90
7PM-10PM (3hrs): served=15, revenue=15×$1.50=$22.50/hr, labor=$30/hr, net/hr=-$7.50, block profit=-$7.50×3=-$22.50

questions.prompt: If you could change the number of baristas during each time period, what would be the optimal daily profit for Marie's Café?
questions.guidance: Candidate should optimize barista count per time block to maximize profit. Key insight: adding a third barista in morning blocks captures more demand (capacity goes to 90); in the evening block, reduce to 1 barista since revenue ($22.50/hr) barely exceeds 1-barista labor ($15/hr). Candidate should also flag the café loses money with 2 baristas in the evening.

math.setup: With 3 baristas, capacity = 90 customers/hour. Optimal barista count minimizes labor while meeting (or matching) demand up to capacity. Net profit/hr = served × $1.50 - baristas × $15.
steps: 10AM-1PM: 3 baristas yield capacity 90, but demand=80, so served=80, profit/hr=80×$1.50-$45=$120-$45=$75, block=$75×3=$225
1PM-4PM: 2 baristas sufficient (demand=60=capacity), same as before, block=$180
4PM-7PM: 1 or 2 baristas; 1 barista capacity=30, profit/hr=30×$1.50-$15=$30, block=$90; 2 baristas capacity=60, served=40, profit/hr=$60-$30=$30, block=$90 — both equivalent

questions.prompt: Marie's Café does not offer wireless access for its customers. Should the café add this service?
questions.guidance: Candidate should evaluate pros and cons across revenue, cost, capacity, and brand dimensions. Strong candidates note the trade-off between attracting more customers/upsell vs. slowing table turnover during busy periods.

questions.prompt: What factors should Marie's Café consider before purchasing an oven to sell pastries?
questions.guidance: This question is triggered if the candidate mentions that competitors sell pastries while Marie's does not. Candidate should think across revenues, costs (fixed and variable), capacity, brand image, and competitive dynamics.

questions.prompt: A new espresso machine priced at $2,000 can decrease average order time from 2 minutes to 90 seconds. How long would it take to pay back the machine?
questions.guidance: With 90-second orders, capacity per barista increases from 30 to 40 orders/hour. Candidate should recalculate optimal daily profit with new throughput and compute payback = machine cost / incremental daily profit. Result: new optimal profit is $922.50/day vs $787.50, incremental = $135/day, payback = $2,000 / $135 ≈ 14.8 days.

math.setup: New capacity per barista = 60 min / 1.5 min = 40 orders/hour. With 2 baristas = 80/hr capacity, 3 baristas = 120/hr. Recalculate optimal profit per block with updated capacity, then compare to $787.50 baseline.
steps: 7AM-10AM: demand=100; 3 baristas capacity=120, served=100, profit/hr=100×$1.50-$45=$105, block=$105×3=$315
10AM-1PM: demand=80; 2 baristas capacity=80, served=80, profit/hr=80×$1.50-$30=$90, block=$90×3=$270
1PM-4PM: demand=60; 2 baristas capacity=80, served=60, profit/hr=60×$1.50-$30=$60, block=$60×3=$180
4PM-7PM: demand=40; 1 barista capacity=40, served=40, profit/hr=40×$1.50-$15=$45, block=$45×3=$135
7PM-10PM: demand=15; 1 barista capacity=40, served=15, profit/hr=15×$1.50-$15=$7.50, block=$7.50×3=$22.50

brainstorming.prompt: Should Marie's Café add wireless internet access?

categories.name: Positives
ideas: Attract more customers who want to work or study in the café
Ability to charge customers for the service as an additional revenue stream
Customers may stay longer and order larger sizes or additional drinks

categories.name: Negatives
ideas: Upfront costs for wireless setup and additional outlets
Space constraints — longer-staying customers reduce table availability
During peak hours, lingering customers slow throughput and reduce revenue
Change in café image — may undermine the cozy, social atmosphere that loyal customers value

recommendation: Optimize staffing levels by time block: add a third barista during morning rush (7AM-10AM) and reduce to one barista in the evening (7PM-10PM) to increase daily profit from $607.50 to $787.50
Invest in the new espresso machine ($2,000) which pays back in ~15 days by increasing throughput and daily profit to $922.50
Shift product mix toward larger sizes and lattes through upselling or eliminating the 8oz size, as larger sizes generate significantly higher margins
risks: Adding staff increases fixed labor costs; benefit only materializes if demand holds at projected levels
Espresso machine requires upfront capital and training; payback assumes demand patterns remain stable
Eliminating small sizes or pushing upsells may alienate price-sensitive customers
next_steps: Pilot the staffing optimization for one week and measure actual customer counts served vs. turned away
Evaluate the espresso machine purchase given the rapid payback period
Assess competitor pastry offerings and feasibility of adding baked goods to expand the menu and increase average transaction value
